MR. WATSON (CHATEAU GUA Y-HUNTINGDON-LAPRAIRIE)-ACTIVITIES OF U.S. INTELLIGENCE AGENCY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a question of personal privilege, on Monday of this week I asked the Solicitor General a question related to reported activities of the Central Intelligence Agency in some international affiliations of the A.F.L.-C.I.O., and I referred with tongue in cheek to possible infiltration of the New Democratic Party by the C.I.A. through the C.L.C.'s international affiliations.
My question arose out of an article which appeared on the front page of the February 20 issue of the Christian Science Monitor. Last night I was amazed to learn that Claude Jodoin, C.L.C. president, had issued a press release which stated in part:
The inference made in the House of Commons by Mr. Ian Watson (Chateauguay-Huntingdon-La-prairie) that unions affiliated to the Canadian Labour Congress may have accepted funds from the Central Intelligence Agency for operations in Canada is completely unjustified.
I would like to make it clear that no such inference was contained in my question. Furthermore, I take strong exception to Mr. Jodoin terming my question unjustified. Despite the apparent attitude of the C.L.C. executive, members of unions in my riding, affiliated with the C.L.C. and international branches of the A.F.L.-C.I.O., are most interested in knowing whether the Central Intelligence Agency has infiltrated Canadian unionism through United States internationals.
Mr. Jodoin in effect is saying that I, as a member of parliament, do not have the right to ask this question. This, Mr. Speaker, is an affront to the basic parliamentary privileges of every member of this house.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we on this side of the house have no intention of causing the least delay in the passing of supplementary estimates with regard to Expo '67.
However, I feel a few comments are necessary and I will only take a few minutes of the time of the committee.
We must remember, Mr. Chairman, that the government is carrying on the work of the Progressive Conservative government, with respect to Expo. In this as in many other endeavours, the present government, is treading a beaten path, in the best interests of Canadians. Our initiatives, while we were in power, continue to have beneficial effects upon the people, and we are happy to see that the government is following in the footsteps of its predecessors, as regards Expo.
Since this is probably our last opportunity to express our views concerning Expo '67, I believe this is the appropriate time to give credit to those concerned. We must admit that the province of Quebec and the city of Montreal owe it to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) for having accepted that Expo '67 be held in the metropolis of Canada. I should also like to mention the contribution of the mayor of the city of Montreal, who co-operated fully. In fact, Mr. Drapeau travelled all over the world playing the part of ambassador; I feel that he also deserves some of the credit due to those responsible for Expo.
Expo '67, Mr. Chairman, is a colossal achievement; it is a monument to science, architecture and engineering. I believe this is the appropriate occasion to recognize the tremendous amount of work done by those who master-minded Expo; this achievement enhances not only their personal reputation, but also the reputation of Canada itself.
The success of Expo will contribute to the success of our country. Expo will play an

important part in making the Canadian people known far beyond our borders. I feel it is essential that we concentrate on making a success of this major event in the life of our country, and it is both a privilege and an honour to belong to a country like Canada.
During the next few months, millions of visitors from all over the world will converge upon our country. If my information is correct-and I believe it is-at least 62 countries have already reserved space at this world exhibition. This, I believe, is the greatest number of countries ever to take part in a world exhibition. This sole consideration, I feel, is reason enough for those who are responsible for Expo to take pride in the work accomplished and expect the operation to be an unqualified success.
Mr. Chairman, Expo is not solely the business of the province of Quebec nor of the city of Montreal. Expo '67 is the business of every Canadian; every Canadian should take an active part in it. This event will bring additional income particularly to the province of Quebec and to the city of Montreal and thus, each will contribute to the prosperity of the other.
We have heard certain remarks on the development and the additional amounts earmarked for Expo. There has been some concern over the fact that the funds voted for Expo have been over-spent; to my mind, this is not surprising, since it was surely most difficult to forecast within a thousand or a hundred dollars, the final cost of the development of Expo '67. Anyone with the slightest experience in construction should be aware that there is often a large gap between the estimated and the actual cost. I had a similar experience last year when I had some repairs done to my home and when the bills came in I was not too surprised to discover that my estimate was doubled. If this is true in private enterprise, it should not be surprising to find the same thing in a public undertaking in which three levels of government are involved, particularly when it is realized that the operations have been carried out over a relatively long period of time.
Mr. Chairman, there are many factors contributing to the increase in the final cost of Expo and even if the cost is much higher than the estimate, according to our information, if it is compared to the cost of development of other world fair sites, the comparison is still to Canada's advantage.
February 24, 1967

[DOT] (11:50 a.m.)
Various factors led to an increase in the cost and even to delays in the development of the Expo site and Expo in general, and the government must be blamed for several of them. They had unfavourable repercussions due to a lack of planning or accuracy on the part of the government.
It is a well known fact that strikes delayed the work and increased the cost, and building materials also cost more. The railway strike and the longshoremen's strike in the Montreal harbour not only delayed the work but had other harmful results. And finally, I would not like to put all the responsibility or blame on the shoulders of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters) and the Minister of Industry and Defence Production (Mr. Drury), but I must point out that the II per cent tax levied by his colleague the Minister of Finance and Receiver General (Mr. Sharp) also had very disastrous results for Expo. Consequently, because of the 11 per cent tax on building materials, the final cost of Expo is greatly increased. The government must take full responsibility for that. Had it not been for that harmful 11 per cent tax whose withdrawal we requested on many occasions, the minister would not have to ask for so much money today. Two months away from the opening of Expo, it would be ill advised to take action which would entail the complete failure of Expo.
I said it and I repeat it: we must do all we can to make sure that Expo '67 will be a big success. The minister must see to that. He is justified to watch closely how public funds are spent.
I do think that the members of my party have full confidence in the minister, as I have. I am sure he will perform his duties with as much care as he can. I ask my colleagues on all sides of the house to say or do nothing that could impede the success of Expo '67, for Canada's image abroad could be eroded.
So let us make Expo '67 our centennial project and let us pool all our efforts and good will so that, through Expo '67, Canada's good name may be echoed in all parts of the globe.

speechtext:
The main purpose of this bill is to revise judicial salaries. The judiciary is such a vital component of our system that any bill dealing with the judiciary is a bill of importance. Salaries of the judiciary have not been revised since August, 1963. The proposed increases are clearly set forth in the bill for those judges for whom parliament has a legislative responsibility under the British North America Act, and require little comment except perhaps to say that an attempt has been made to fix judicial salaries at such a level as will permit the maintenance of the very high
Judges Act
standard of our judiciary without at the same time creating any question of doubt that those who do serve in this way do so out of a profound sense of and desire for public service. Percentage or uniform increases are not being proposed. Rather, an attempt has been made to increase salaries where justified in relation to the importance of the duties and responsibilities connected with the judicial office.
[DOT] (12:10 p.m.)
In addition to the general increases we are proposing we also are making provision for the payment of an additional salary of $2,000 subject to certain specified conditions. Speaking generally, this additional sum is to be paid to all judges except those who receive from a province any annual or periodic compensation as a judge of a superior or county court. In certain provinces such as British Columbia, Alberta and Ontario, judges do receive payments in varying amounts as judges of the superior or county courts. New section 20 of clause 1 will not deprive them of these provincial payments, but if they continue to receive them they will not receive the additional salary provided by parliament. In this way an attempt is being made to equalize the salaries paid to the holders of these important provincial judicial offices. It is not easy, Mr. Speaker, to formulate the criteria by which judicial salaries should be assessed. The government have given the matter sustained consideration and have come to the conclusion that the amounts are on the whole reasonable and fair.
In addition to the salary revisions the bill deals with one or two matters that should be mentioned. We are proposing to broaden the law relating to travelling allowances. In essence, the proposed changes will permit judges to be paid their actual expenses when they travel on official business as judges, whether they travel to hold court, to sit in chambers or for any other official purpose. We are also proposing some estate tax relief for the widows of judges who receive annuities under the act. The proposed new provision is for all practical purposes the same as the one found in the Public Service Superannuation Act as amended in 1960, and the intention is to deal with the tax payable on pensions of judges' widows in the same way as pensions payable to public servants.
Finally, we are proposing to broaden the provisions of the law to make it clear that

February 24, 1967
Judges Act
judges can act as commissioners or arbitrators, etc., if there is either a federal or provincial statute authorizing them to do so, as well as in cases where, as at present, there is proper executive authority from the governor or lieutenant governor in council. However, judges who do undertake these special duties will be permitted to receive only their actual travelling and other expenses while away from their ordinary places of residence, if these expenses are paid by the governments concerned.
It will be seen that judges will still be permitted to engage in extrajudicial duties in proper cases, but that they will not receive anything more for doing so than they would have received had they been performing their ordinary judicial functions. The result will be that judges who do undertake extrajudicial duties cannot be accused of doing so for pecuniary motives or personal gain at the expense of their brother judges who in some cases are required to assume additional judicial burdens as a result.
Before concluding, Mr. Speaker, I should give notice that when the house comes to clause 4 I shall seek an amendment for the purpose of clarifying the provisions respecting annuities. The amendment, to put the matter shortly, will clarify the fact that the salary of the judge for the purpose of calculating the annuity includes the amount of any additional salary provided by new section 20 of clause 1.

Mr. Speaker, next only to freedom of debate in this parliament the independence of the judiciary is the cornerstone of our Canadian democracy and our freedoms. Founded upon the Act of Settlement, the principle of judicial independence is a gift of Britain to the democratic world second only in importance to her gift of parliamentary institutions.
Judicial independence means, in my submission, simply that judicial functions should be performed in an atmosphere in which there is no hope of gain or preferment on the one hand, and no fear of punishment, intimidation, restraint, discipline or retribution on the other. The judge must be in a position where he can fearlessly uphold the law and the cause of justice without being influenced in any way by the effect of his decisions on his own personal career or fortunes. Norman Ward in the fourth edition of Dawson's "The Government of Canada" puts it rather neatly at page 449:
The judge is placed in a position where he has nothing to lose by doing what is right and little

to gain by doing what is wrong; and there is therefore every reason to hope that his best efforts will be devoted to the conscientious performance of his duty.
On the same page the learned author in one short paragraph epitomizes the Canadian concept of the judiciary, and I venture to quote this paragraph:
The judge will thus usually begin with the twin assets of character and ability, and these become the foundation on which the indirect appeals are based. He is paid a substantial salary, which not only removes some of the obvious temptations, but frees him from financial distractions. The importance of his office is continually stressed; his own rectitude and sense of fairness are invariably assumed; the dignity of the court and the respect accorded his office are rarely, if ever, challenged; his social position is always assured. These efforts to accentuate the eminence of the office are made infinitely more effective by the fortunate regard which the legal profession has for the judiciary and its ingrained habit of regarding a seat on the bench as the crown of a legal career. Thus some of the very men who build up the tradition may be induced to accept judgeships a few years later, influenced to a material degree by the tradition which they themselves have helped to create. Not the least important result of this prestige is its effect on the public, who have come to accept it-[DOT] and with some justification-at its face value, and who see in judicial independence a greater promise of justice than could be obtained through the application of ordinary political sanctions.
As I see it, the intention of this bill is to uphold and strengthen these precepts which are so clearly set forth, and in that light it must be tested. Canadians at all levels of income concede readily that judges of all courts should be paid such salaries and provided with such pensions for themselves and their dependants as will assure not only full financial independence but will be attractive to leaders of the bar to accept judicial appointment; for without financial independence other aspects of independence are illusory or hallucinatory.
It becomes a matter of judgment as to what the levels of salary must be to achieve those universally accepted objectives. For myself, I believe that if there is to be error it should be on the side of generosity. When we are in committee of the whole we can examine in detail with the Solicitor General the scale of salaries proposed by the bill, ascertain more closely than he has stated on second reading the principles upon which the figures are based, and decide then upon their wisdom. Consequently at this stage I refrain from detailed comment upon the salary levels proposed.
But I believe I should point out that there is an ever-growing problem of persuading

Personally I hope that never again will a justice of the Supreme Court of Canada be appointed to any royal commission at any time. You will remember, Mr. Speaker, that I have on the order paper private members' Bill C-237, which would have the effect of preventing any judge of the Supreme Court of Canada from accepting any extra judicial appointment. In arbitration, conciliation and mediation work in employer-employee relations it is exceedingly difficult for a judge to avoid being tagged as either a labour man or a company man. It is hard for him to avoid public attacks as a result of his activities. Indeed, the constant use of judges for arbitration and conciliation has, at least in the province of Ontario, divided the bench into the "haves" and the "have nots". The

"haves" are those who are regularly engaged in outside non-judicial assignments at worthwhile fees, and the "have nots" are those whose talents are not sought in this field or those who on principle refuse to accept nonjudicial work.
My hope is that this legislation will result in actually restricting judges to their judicial knitting. It is true that there will have to be panels of arbitrators, mediators or conciliators, but I suggest they will have to be created from the non-judicial world, from the academic world, from members of the bar and elsewhere. I suggest most earnestly that judges must be sent back to their courtrooms. If this is the by-product of these increases and of other amendments in the bill, it will be most worth-while in the national interest.
My views on the excellence of the Canadian judiciary have been frequently expressed in this chamber and I do not intend to repeat them this morning. Without necessarily approving the particular increases or the scale of increases proposed by the bill, we welcome any legislation which will strengthen the independence and impartiality of the Canadian judiciary, for thereby we strengthen the nation.

Mr. Speaker, I want to make a very brief point to the Solicitor General, and my point is this. A separation recently took place in Nova Scotia with the creation of an appeal division with three judges and a trial division with six judges. At the moment nine judges replace a system which employed seven judges. The arithmetic of this change has had the effect of removing one of the trial judges, and I suggest this is something the Solicitor General and the attorney general of Nova Scotia might well wish to consider, perhaps after some consultation with the newly appointed chief justice of the appeal division, Hon. L. D. Currie, who was recently chief justice in the trial division and who would therefore be aware of the problem which had been created.

The reason this problem is a little acute at the present time is that it frequently happens that one of the three appeal judges has to remove himself from hearing an appeal because of his involvement in the case when it came on for trial. There are also other reasons why one of the members of a three man appeal court may feel he should not be sitting on a certain appeal. This can be remedied by bringing up a judge from the trial division to fill in on a temporary basis and hear the appeal, but this has the effect of putting more pressure on the judges of the trial division. I think this is a matter the Solicitor General and the attorney general of Nova Scotia should consider, I suggest in consultation with the chief justice of the appeal division and other judges as well.
I should like to make a further point, one which has been made several times and made very well by the hon. member for Carleton. There is a group of judges who do not partake of extra-judicial functions such as sitting as conciliators, mediators and the like, and this has created the rather awesome burden of trying to keep the court calendars and trial work up to date.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that we seriously consider that judicial independence of judges means much more than financial independence. It should also mean that none of them is put in the position of carrying such a work load that his ability to deal properly with cases is impaired because there is simply too much work to do.

Mr. Chairman, before dealing with some of the questions raised by the hon. member for Carleton I wish to compliment him on the eloquent address he made, and to concur in general with his remarks about the judiciary and the sacrifices they make in accepting an appointment to the bench. The hon. member mentioned the case of Lord Kilmuir, and that Lord Kilmuir while a practising member of the bar was earning $115,000 per annum. The recent increase in the salaries of high court judges in the United Kingdom brings the salary of a high court judge up to $30,000, which confirms the point made by the hon. member.
As I stated earlier, Mr. Chairman, it is not easy to formulate the criteria by which judicial salaries should be assessed. It is not done on a percentage basis or by an across the board increase. We try to even it out according to the responsibilities of the office. The supreme court judges will receive between $28,000 and $30,000, depending on the province in which they serve. This compares with the figure of $30,000 in Great Britain I mentioned a moment ago.
So far as the county court and district court judges are concerned a difficult problem arises. The salaries paid county court judges under provincial legislation are such that in some provinces the additional salary is caught by clause 20 while in other provinces it is not. In other words, Mr. Chairman, the salary paid by the provinces in some cases is free from the deduction of $2,000.
Perhaps I may put it in another way. I believe that in some provinces the county court judges will receive, over and above anything that is paid to them under the federal statute, the amount paid to them under the provincial statute. In other provinces they will have to forgo the amount paid to them under the provincial statute if they accept the full amount under the federal statute. So no matter what course we adopted we were still going to have disparity in the salaries of county court judges across the country.
I did have the pleasure of meeting with a number of representatives of the county court judges, Mr. Chairman, and I appreciate the problem. I suggested at the time that I enter
Judges Act
into private consultation with the attorneys general of the various provinces to see whether the provincial legislatures will consider amending their statutes to enable the federal government to bring uniformity to the salaries of county and district court judges. On reflection I would say, with respect, that this seems to me perhaps to be the most desirable way in which to approach this rather difficult subject.
The hon. member for Carleton also raised the point about pensions and with genuine concern suggested we should be 'a little more generous in this connection. The government was perhaps a little reluctant to move any further under this bill, because in fairness I think the pensions of all public servants should be considered and given equal study before any action is taken. There has been study of this point from time to time.

I believe the hon. member for Carleton dealt effectively with the question raised by the hon. member for Roberval. I am not sure the minister has dealt effectively with the point I made about the disparity between salaries paid to supreme court and county court judges in the province of Ontario. The position, as I understand it, is that both receive an amount from the province, so neither bench would be entitled to draw anything under clause 20, the extra $2,000, unless the legislature amends the existing legislation.
The position is that the supreme court judges draw an amount of $4,000 from the Ontario legislature, and the county judges get $3,500. This in fact increases the disparity between the two benches; there is an increase of $5,000 for the supreme court and $3,000 for the county court. This represents a widening of the disparity, whereas in my opinion the reverse should be the case. I am not sure that the Solicitor General and the Minister of Justice have dealt as generously with the county judges, relatively, as they should have done in the circumstances.
I understand that the minister intends as a concomitant to introduce an amendment whereby pensions will be based upon an amount including the $2,000. In my opinion the minister should give more consideration to the position of the county court judges.

speechtext:
I appreciate the point made by the hon. member for Carleton. Perhaps I can elaborate on the question. The county court judges receive from the province $3,500 and, if I am correct, this covers their duties as surrogate court judges. I respectfully suggest that if the provincial act was drafted so that they received say $2,500 as surrogate court judges and $1,000 for county court duties, the $2,500 set aside for surrogate duties would not be

caught by the clause we have been considering. This would be an effective way of bringing the salaries of Ontario county court judges closer to those of high court judges.
If we were to adopt any other approach it would mean that in provinces where the provincial statute is drafted so that the amount paid is not caught by the provisions of clause 20, the county court judges in that province would be receiving an amount much closer to the supreme court scales than in other provinces, and we would still have the problem of disparity.

I wish to touch on this distinction between county or district court judges and supreme court judges. My view is that the situation in Quebec is far better than it is in other provinces. There is often an inclination among some people to measure the quality of justice which litigants receive by the extent of the jurisdiction possessed by the judges, and sometimes this involves the question of salaries. One of the difficulties the Solicitor General faces is that the extent of a judge's duties is fixed largely by the provincial legislatures. It is my feeling that this might be the subject of discussion at a conference of attorneys general looking toward the removal of the barriers which now exist.

Mr. Chairman, before this committee in its infinite wisdom decided at one o'clock there were better places for hon. members to spend their time than in committee, I had been dealing with the distinctions between supreme court and country court judges. I said that I admired the system prevailing in Quebec where there is no distinction between judges. There superior court judges deal with matters which in other provinces are divided between supreme court and county court judges. It is for the provinces and not for the federal government to say how the courts shall be organized and how they shall deal with their work. I hope that at some time this subject may be discussed at the meetings which take place between the Solicitor General, the Minister of Justice and the Attorneys General. I think it is desirable that the ultimate objective of having no distinction between judges be achieved.
While we are not allowed to say what proceedings have taken place in committee it is no secret that in the joint committee on divorce where we have been considering proposed changes in our divorce laws most of the briefs which have been presented and made public have shown the wisdom of conferring the right to dissolve marriages on county, district and supreme court judges. As work piles up it will be most desirable to bring together under one judge the jurisdiction of supreme court and district court judges, leaving the provinces free rein as to the way estate and surrogate work and debt collection are handled.
Another point I wish to talk about is dealt with in clause 1. I refer to the payment of the additional $2,000 which is to be included in
Judges Act
the new section 20 of the Judges Act. New section 20 in part reads as follows:
-an additional salary of $2,000.00 per annum as compensation for any extra-judicial services-
I take it that the extra work referred to is extra work which the judges will perform as judges. I also take it that this follows the recommendations made over a number of years by the public accounts committee. For a number of years that committee, during examination of the Auditor General's report, has commented about supreme court, county and district court judges having been assigned to extrajudicial duties as conciliators, members of arbitration boards and so on. They have received $40, $50 or even $100 a day, ostensibly earmarked as living and travelling expenses. I feel that these payments have contained an element of remuneration. The view that the Auditor General and the public accounts committee have consistently taken for four or five years is that payments of this kind do contain an element of remuneration. Both the persons who received this money and the government which approved payment thereof would therefore be in direct violation of the Judges Act as it then stood, because that act provides that apart from his salary no judge should receive any remuneration.
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
During the hearings of the committee we had the pleasure of having the deputy minister of justice appear before us to give us his view, but quite frankly I might say that we were not satisfied. However, as I understand it this clause will now cover that situation. It was not that we objected to judges receiving these payments but rather that we objected to their receiving them in the way in which they did, since they contain an element of remuneration. There is ample justification for them. It has been brought to our attention that in some cases judges who have received such payments have filed income tax returns in which they included a portion of the $60 or $100 a day they had received allegedly as living allowance. In their income tax returns they included part of these amounts as income.
I think this provision brings to an end a very undesirable situation. As the hon. member for Carleton pointed out, a distinction was created between judges because while some judges engaged in this type of work and received very substantial additional remuneration their colleagues on the bench were compelled to carry out most of the judicial duties.

I hope that the attempt to introduce what can only be described as an element of remuneration in the living and travelling allowances of judges engaged in extrajudicial duties will now cease.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member has raised what one might almost call the annual question which comes before the house whenever we are dealing with matters related to the judiciary. Without in any way reflecting upon what considerations may have entered into the appointment of judges before I assumed any responsibility in that regard, I wish to assure the house that the number one consideration to my knowledge has been the experience, character and learning of the person who is appointed to the bench. I would be less than frank, however, if I said there were no other considerations, but I wish to emphasize that to the best of my knowledge the primary considerations have been the character and learning of the individual. I might go further to indicate that in my experience inquiries have been discreetly made about the individual concerned and as to whether or not he has ever been before the dicipline committees of the various law societies. Generally speaking the person who is appointed has been endorsed by a bencher or other high ranking member of the Law Society. However, to speak more seriously, I will say that I have every respect for the judiciary of this country regardless of whether they were appointed by the previous Conservative government or by the Liberal government. I believe that no reflection should be cast on the judiciary.
There may be the odd occasion when a problem arises but after all judges are human beings just the same as any other person. I am sure that if you explore any party, fraternal organization, service club or church you will find people who are not acting in the way they should. Once again let me say that when the day comes that the present Solicitor General ceases to hold his office, surely the fact that he was a Liberal cabinet minister and served his party and the country well will not prevent him from receiving any type of appointment in the judiciary. Of course I am not buttering him up because I am trying

to get something out of him as there is very little that he can do for me or my constituency. If he were the Minister of Public Works or the Minister of Transport I might be doing so, but this is another matter.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. First of all I wish to say that I thank the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria for his generous remarks. I should say, with sincerity, that if the illustration had been left to me I could have looked across the floor of the house and picked better examples.
I should like to move an amendment which reads as follows:
That clause 1 of Bill C-267, An Act to amend the Judges Act, be amended by adding thereto the following subclause:
(3) Sections 4 to 7 and sections 9 to 19 of the said Act as enacted by this section shall be deemed to have come into force on the 1st day of March, 1967.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
The purpose of the amendment is to permit judges who retire between March 1 and June of this year to have their pensions calculated on the increased salary. In the case of a county court judge it would be $19,000 but it would not include the additional $2,000 which is established by the new section 20.
May I ask if this provision would assist the widow of the late chief justice of Nova Scotia with her pension? I hope it would.

I regret to advise the hon. member that it is my understanding it would not. It would only cover those who retire between March 1 and June 1. There has to be a cut-off period, and whatever period is chosen it works to the disadvantage of some otherwise deserving individual. This is an unfortunate fact of life.

speechtext:
Shall the amendment carry?
Amendment (Mr. Sharp) agreed to.

There are two matters I should like to mention. The minister has by his amendment taken care of the increase in the number of judges in British Columbia. Doubtless he will have observed from the

morning newspaper that first reading was given yesterday in the legislature of Ontario to a bill to increase the number of judges of the high court to 26. Does the minister think he might take judicial notice of the legislation and perhaps seek an amendment now so we would not have to come back to this matter on another occasion? We would be prepared to have the resolution adopted by unanimous consent to cover the particular situation.
The other situation is that this proposed new section 20 has been exempted from the amendment just carried. Will the minister indicate why he has chosen the 1st day of June, 1967 as the operative date for the proposed new section 20?

If I may deal with the last question first, Mr. Chairman, the date of June 1 was selected to give the judges an opportunity to make an election as to whether they preferred to receive the additional salary under new section 20 or reject it and accept the allowance from the province. This date also permits the provinces a period in which they may revise their own legislation if they so desire dealing with the point raised earlier in the debate.
In so far as the first point is concerned, I am grateful for the spirit of co-operation manifested by the hon. member for Carleton. If I am hesitant about accepting his suggestion, it is only because I am not satisfied that all the steps have been taken in connection with the provincial legislation. It might be somewhat presumptuous on our part to take steps here when there are still certain formalities to be cleared in the provincial legislature. I do appreciate the offer of co-operation.
Clause as amended agreed to.
Clauses 2 and 3 agreed to.
On clause 4-Regulations re payment of inheritance taxes, etc.

I seek to make an amendment to clause 4. The amendment I seek would mean that the present proposed new section 30 in clause 4 would be renumbered new section 30A and there would be a new proposed section 30 which would read as follows:
30. For the purposes of the provisions of this act respecting annuities, there shall be included in the salary of which a judge was in receipt under this act at any time after the coming into force of section 20, the amount of any additional salary provided for by that section whether or not at that time such additional salary was being paid to him.
February 24, 1967

Then, of course, this would be followed by the renumbering of the present proposed section 30 as 30A. The purpose of the amendment is to clarify the fact that the pension of a judge will be calculated on his salary, including the additional salary that is paid to him under new section 20. If I may use an illustration, because the basic increase is $3,000 a county court judge will receive $19,000. Then, according to new section 20, he will be paid an additional $2,000 which will bring his salary up to $21,000.
Since certain provinces are paying their judges an additional salary the judge has to make an election. Either he accepts the $2,000 under this provision or he accepts the additional salary payable under the provincial legislation. The county court judge would receive the basic $3,000 increase bringing his salary to $19,000. I would expect that most of them in Ontario would prefer to accept the $3,500 from the province rather than the $2,000 provided under the new section 20. This would bring their gross salary up to $22,500. However, their pensions will be calculated on $21,000 so that every county court judge in Canada will have his pension calculated on the common figure of $21,000. This amendment was introduced because there was some doubt expressed whether it was clear the additional salary of $2,000 was included in the amount for calculation of pension.

I gather from what the minister has said that if this amendment were not introduced there might be a difference between the judges in one province and another. In one province the calculation could have been on the basis of $21,000 and in another province it could conceivably have been on the basis of $19,000. This amendment will make the basis of calculation uniform across the country.
The hon. member for Carleton has put the matter succinctly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I so move.
Amendment (Mr. Sharp) agreed to.
Clause as amended agreed to.
On clause 5-Acting as commissioner, etc.

I should like to come back to the general matter of the acceptance by judges of appointments to extrajudicial functions. I fully support the position taken in this matter by the hon. member for Carleton and I certainly support any moves such as are
Judges Act
reflected in this bill to discourage the acceptance by judges of appointments to nonjudicial functions. However, I do not believe the bill goes far enough. Accordingly I have an amendment to offer to clause 5 which I think would carry this provision a further step along the way.
The general arguments against acceptance by judges of appointments to extrajudicial functions have been made already, so I will not do more than summarize them. They are first, that with the pressure of litigation and business which is properly the function of judges this practice imposes an extra burden on those judges who do not take such appointments. It is also unfair to litigants when delays occur because judges are not available to dispose of their cases.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
An equally undesirable result is that the way we have been inclined to appoint judges to boards and commissions-I use the word "we" advisedly; I am not singling out any government-has brought them into political controversy and has lowered the standing and reputation of the bench. The outstanding example, of course, has already been referred to by the hon. member for Carleton, the inquiry of which Mr. Justice Spence was appointed commissioner. But there are other cases where we have been all too prone to appoint judges as chairmen of conciliation and arbitration boards and to make appointments of the kind where the judge in question is bound to be criticized by one or both parties to a dispute. In addition, where awards are bound to come back to parliament or to one of the legislatures and be subjected to political controversy or political settlement, judges are brought into relationship with the parties in a role they should not have, and also inevitably into the centre of political dispute.
I feel very strongly, Mr. Chairman, that both the federal and provincial authorities should be precluded from so appointing judges. I remember that when I was minister I said to myself that I would not do it, that I was opposed to it in principle, but without a legislative prohibition the pressure-if you like, the habit-was such that I was not able to resist the trend as successfully as I had intended and as I had hoped. I am quite satisfied that whatever may be the approach in principle on the part of the Solicitor General and his colleague, the hon. gentleman will also be unable to resist the pressure

February 24, 1967
Judges Act
unless there is a stronger legislative prohibition than the one presently contained in the bill.
Clause 5 actually proposes, in my view, a weakening of the restraint on the appointment of judges to this kind of function because it removes the requirement that the consent of the governor in council of Canada be obtained before a judge can accept such an appointment. While not a prohibition, it provided at least some restraint. I think that we should in fact go further, and provide that neither federal nor provincial levels of government may make this kind of use of members of the judiciary unless the appointment is specifically authorized by a statute of the federal parliament or one of the provincial legislatures. I do not think there should be the discretion which this clause still contemplates leaving to the governor in council or lieutenant-governor in council in making an appointment even though the appointment in question may not be authorized by statute.
If you amend the bill to prohibit appointments without specific statutory authorization in the first place, you would have the protection of inertia; you would have to introduce legislation to authorize an appointment. It would of course be possible to amend the labour code here and in the provinces, but this would be subject to the natural disinclination to introduce legislation into busy legislative assemblies.
In the second place, the attention of the members of the legislatures would in each case be directed to the propriety of authorizing judges to serve in the capacity which the legislation might contemplate. I would hope and expect that the legislators in both provincial and federal parliaments would accept the principle that except in special and rare cases judges should not be asked to assume duties which are not part of their ordinary judicial function, and for the reasons I have outlined; so that they would look critically at any such proposed legislation.
There is one particular aspect of this matter that I want to mention. It is frequently said, at times when this principle is being discussed and the point of view I have put forward is under consideration, that it would be very difficult to carry on the process of labour conciliation and arbitration unless we had judges available to serve as chairmen of arbitration and conciliation boards. I think, Mr. Chairman-I hope the minister will agree with me, and I think the members of the

committee will-that in the present atmosphere it has become quite evident that the bench is indeed being brought into disrepute because of the dislike of labour unions in particular for the kind of decision which is given in these adjudications. We now have labour leaders declaring they have no confidence in the impartiality of the bench. That is a statement which, of course, I absolutely reject. There is no foundation for it; but it is symptomatic of a very undesirable situation and is proof positive of the fact that because of the use being made of the judiciary in these extrajudicial functions the bench is suffering a loss of reputation, of regard and of stature in the community.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I think it becomes an inescapable and an urgent responsibility of this parliament to act to prevent any further development along those lines. I think it is incumbent upon this parliament and this government, as well as upon provincial legislatures, instead of following blindly this pattern of reaching out and asking judges to accept this kind of appointment, rather to build up a panel of permanent chairmen within the cadre of the labour departments, both federal and provincial, who will be available for appointment at a moment's notice as chairmen of conciliation and arbitration boards. In this way we would establish a group of people who will acquire an expertise and a skill in the issues involved in industrial disputes and who will have the confidence of both sides to such disputes.
This would be a most important and I think essential beginning toward a system of having not only chairmen of arbitration boards available but of building up a permanent judicial process for dealing with labour disputes. It would be a judicial process although not part of the present court system. Indeed, I think labour disputes should be dealt with by a separate judicial process which would have the confidence from the outset of both sides to disputes and would also have the result that adjudications would protect the interests of society as well.
For these reasons, Mr. Chairman, I think it is essential that we now make a firm legislative prohibition against the appointment of judges to these kinds of functions, and I therefore move:
That clause 5 of the bill be amended as follows:
1.	By deleting from the proposed section 38 (1) (a) the words "or he is thereunto appointed or so authorized by the Governor in Council" where they appear in lines 24 and 25;
February 24, 1967

2.	By deleting from the proposed section 38 (1) (b) the words "or he is thereunto appointed or so authorized by the Lieutenant-Governor in Council of the province" where they appear in lines 29 to 32;
3.	By adding the following as subsection (2) of section 38:
"(2) This section does not apply in any case where a judge was appointed commissioner, arbitrator, adjudicator, referee, conciliator or mediator before the coming into force of this section".
As you will appreciate, Mr. Chairman, the effect of the first part of the amendment would be to take out the power otherwise expressly reserved to the governor in council to appoint or authorize the services of a judge in these non-judicial capacities. The second part would remove the similar authority given the lieutenant-governor in council of a province. So unless the appointment were authorized with respect to matters within federal jurisdiction expressly by a statute of the parliament of Canada, a judge could not be appointed, or in the case of matters within provincial jurisdiction, if my amendment carries such appointment would have to be expressly authorized by a statute of the legislature. It would not be open to the governor in council to exercise a discretion and to reach out and make an appointment of a judge to a conciliation or arbitration board unless the appointment was so authorized by statute.
The effect of the third part of the amendment would be simply to preserve the appointment and authority of any judge who had been appointed before the amendment comes into effect. I would not want to go so far as to render nugatory anything that had been done under an appointment that was hitherto legal. The effect of the amendment, therefore, would be that when presently appointed judges have completed their work no such appointment could be made in future unless expressly authorized by statute.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
I hope the minister will accept the spirit and purpose of the amendment. There may be some technical flaws in it. If there are and if he will point them out to me, I will be glad to accept modifications which achieve the purpose sought. But I believe it to be clear and acceptable in principle that judges should not be allowed to accept these appointments unless they are specifically authorized by a statute of the parliament of Canada or of the provincial legislatures.

I appreciate the spirit in which the amendment is proposed. As I understand it, the purpose is, first of all, that the time of judges should be conserved by ceasing
Judges Act
to employ judges in non-judicial capacities and, in the second place, that judges should not be called upon in connection with labour disputes unless statutory authority is given by an act of parliament or of the legislatures.
Though the intention is a worthy one I cannot but think of a recent experience in the province of Saskatchewan if I remember correctly where both parties to a dispute made a request of the Attorney General that a particular judge be appointed to deal with it because of the special confidence they felt in him. It seems to me that if we were to agree to the amendment proposed by the hon. member we should no longer find it possible to accede to a reasonable request of this nature.
I agree, that the occasions on which the governor in council or the lieutenant governors in council should call on judges to undertake non-judicial duties ought to be restricted to a bare minimum. As the hon. member suggested, such appointments do expose judges to risks of the kind he mentioned. However, I believe we should continue to give the governor in council and the lieutenant governors authority to appoint judges on the rare occasions when it would be clearly be in the public interest to do so. When both parties request a particular judge, surely we should not deny a course of action which might quickly settle a dispute. Otherwise it might drag on for months.

To deal with the minister's brief reply, may I suggest to him that the illustration he has given does not really support his argument or weaken the proposition I have advanced. I suggest to the minister in all seriousness that if a judge could not be appointed in the case he mentioned the parties would readily have agreed on someone else, especially if the provinces were encouraged to build up panels of permanent chairmen as part of the cadres of their labour departments.
If we do not stop appointing judges we shall never build up these cadres of men who will be available for appointment as chairmen of these boards. We can go on saying that there are all sorts of particular cases where judges would be suitable, but if judges could not serve others could be found. It is the principle which is important here and I do not see how the principle can be preserved except by agreeing to an amendment such as I have moved.

February 24, 1967
Judges Act

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we do not often get an opportunity to speak in committee of the whole with so many faces opposite. It is a temptation which is difficult to resist, now that so many members have come in.
We understand the motives behind the amendment moved by the hon. member for Kamloops and we are in agreement with some of the things he said when introducing it. Obviously that is a prelude to suggesting there is something to be said on the other side. We agree that the load placed on the judiciary because of the acceptance of these outside appointments is perhaps a heavy one and that the services of judges should be used sparingly for this kind of work, or maybe there should be more judges.
We also agree that there are certain kinds of inquiry to which the appointment of judges is not desirable because they do not add to the respect with which the judiciary is held by the public. At the same time, I believe the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Kamloops goes too far. I do not agree with him that a hard and fast line can be drawn between the kind of issues which get into the courts and the kind of issues which never get into the courts of the land but which require judicial and impartial determination.
The standard complaint to make, of course, is that judges should not be used in connection with labour disputes. I submit there are occasions when a labour dispute is just as important as any issue which comes into a court. There are times, as the Solicitor General has pointed out, when both sides feel that the resolution of a dispute can best be made by someone with the experience of a judge, by someone who has the reputation for impartiality which goes with sitting on the bench.
I think the kind of warning which has been sounded against appointing judges to a good many of these boards and so on is one which should be sounded. But it is not a good principle to say that judges should never be available for employment in connection with labour disputes or special problems which may arise in our country.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
I believe that the actual wording of the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Kamloops is too ironclad. It leaves no loopholes for a special circumstance. An issue might arise in a provincial or national setting when the legislature or parliament is not in session to pass the necessary act. If the

amendment as proposed were carried there would no no possibility, even by order in council, of appointing a member of the bench to one of these positions mentioned, no matter how badly he might be needed.
I am ready to say that the kind of warning sounded on this matter is good, but I believe the amendment goes too far. We shall vote against it.
Amendment (Mr. Fulton) negatived: Yeas, 27; nays, 50.

Before the clause carries could the minister say what acts of the parliament of Canada at the present tune expressly authorize a judge to act as a commissioner, arbitrator, adjudicator, referee, conciliator or mediator? When the bill was drafted the minister obviously must have known what these acts were. I think the committee should know the precise authority under existing statutes.
I am sure the hon. member would not expect me to carry a list of the acts with me. I do not have such list. Speaking from memory, I believe the municipal act says that the county court may act.
That is a provincial act and I spoke of acts of the parliament of Canada.

The clause refers to federal and provincial legislation. There is the Expropriation Act, and other acts. I could cite a number of provincial acts giving power to judges to act as arbitrator and adjudicator. The power is given to the county court of the county in which the action arises.

With respect, the minister has not mentioned a single act of the parliament of Canada. He did refer to the Expropriation Act but matters dealt with under that act come by way of information laid before the Exchequer Court of Canada. The proceeding is entirely judicial. It is not an inquiry. There is no mediator or conciliator there.
I have no doubt that before the bill was drafted the minister was fully aware of the acts. The officials in his department would know the acts of parliament relevant to my question and would inform the minister. The acts I refer to are not provincial acts. I do not think it is our business to delve into the
February 24, 1967

provincial situation, but I think we should know what the minister understood on the advice of his officials.

I believe the Inquiries Act is a federal act and provides that a judge may act. I always try to be perfectly frank with the house. In all my nakedness I stand here; I cannot give the hon. member specific acts. The validity and the force of this clause do not turn on the Solicitor General's ability to name specific acts. I am satisfied that if this matter were not dealt with in the manner we have dealt with it the effect would be to jeopardize future actions by the lieutenant governors and governor in council in legitimate circumstances.

The minister is confusing things and confusing me. He speaks of action taken by the lieutenant governor or the governor in council. That is not the point. The minister has spoken of the Inquiries Act. That act provides for the appointment of a commissioner. It does not say that the commissioner shall be a judge. There is nothing in that act which is express authority to a judge to act. With great respect, the Inquiries Act is not relevant to my question.
I am not trying to embarrass the Solicitor General. He has brilliant officials in the gallery. I cannot understand why he did not bring them to the floor of the house to assist him. I was glad to see that the President of the Treasury Board had no such inhibition earlier this week. The Solicitor General is asking the committee to approve this clause without saying what are the acts of parliament which expressly authorize a judge to act as commissioner, arbitrator, adjudicator, referee, conciliator or mediator on any inquiry, commission or other proceeding, to use the exact language of the clause.
That language was not included in the draft idly. Obviously somebody must have studied the situation and said: "These are the statutes where there is express provision to do these things." This has nothing to do with the power of the governor in council.
I do not want to delay the legislation because I approve of it in general, with the exception of this clause. I ask the minister to undertake to give me a list of the acts of parliament I asked for in the very near future and before this bill has had royal assent.

Mr. Chairman, I find the hon. member's request reasonable. He has cooperated well in the passage of this bill and I
Judges Act
cannot take exception to anything he has said. I am pleased to give the undertaking he requests.
