speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Minister of Finance) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-270, to amend the Small Businesses Loans Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, first I should like to thank hon. members of this house for the
13458	COMMONS
Small Businesses Loans Act Amendment very unexpected and very welcome applause. I expected it from this side of the house, but from the other side it is a particular pleasure.
I wish to express my deep gratitude.
At the resolution stage my parliamentary secretary gave a description of the purpose of the bill which is before us. His remarks will be found in Hansard for February 16 beginning at page 13139. I do not intend to repeat what he said and I am sure the house would not expect me to do so.
I should like to make a brief summary. The bill extends the Small Businesses Loans Act for another three year period. It already has been in effect for six years. At the same time it enlarges the application of the act by broadening the purposes for which guaranteed loans may be made. The principal changes are as follows: First, to enable the owner of a retail store to obtain a loan to finance the purchase of the building in which he is located. This removes an anomaly which existed in the present act. I am sure that everyone would wish this anomaly removed. Previously the owner could purchase premises across the road but could not buy the building in which he was located. The second change enables loans to be made to small business enterprises in the construction, transportation and communications industries as well as in manufacturing, wholesale and retail trade and services. The third change is to amend the definition of an eligible small business enterprise as one whose estimated annual gross revenue does not exceed $500,000. The limitation in the present act is $250,000.
These amendments, I believe, will enable the Small Businesses Loans Act to make a greater contribution to the needs of small enterprises in this country.

Mr. Speaker, we appreciate the brief introduction the minister has just given us to the bill now before us. We have very little more to say at this time, since many members of our party spoke on this legislation when it was at the resolution stage. At that time they expressed their general support for the bill and for what this act had done in the past. They were very much in accord with the changes, particularly in view of the fact that we introduced this type of legislation in 1961 when we were the government. We have been glad to see this act amended once or twice previously and we now are glad to see it revised once more so that it will become more applicable to the needs of the small businessman who certainly requires such support. Other points will be

DEBATES	February 24, 1967
discussed when we reach the clause by clause consideration of the bill. Therefore I do not propose to hold up the progress of the bill at this time.

Mr. Speaker, I shall be quite brief at this time, which is my usual practice. We support the principle behind the proposed amendments. I remember that prior to the introduction of this legislation by the Conservative government in 1961 small business organizations throughout the country had made frequent requests for legislation of this type. I do not think there is any doubt that this is good legislation. At this time I cannot resist at least congratulating the former government for introducing it into the house in 1961. Since that time there have been several amendments as a result of experience and I think that generally the act has proven to be very satisfactory.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
I am very interested in the application of the act. I have had conversations with many bank managers in my constituency, particularly in the smaller communities. I have found them most co-operative. They did not lend money unless there was a sound basis for the loan but they were co-operative in that they were anxious to do what they could to assist the smaller businessman. I have here the fifth annual report on operations under the Small Businesses Loans Act for the year ended December 31, 1965. To show how sound in principle this program is I should like to read this paragraph:
Since inception to December 31,	1965,	14,050
loans amounting to over $127 million were made by the banks under this legislation. During this period payments have been made to the banks under the guarantee provision in respect of 25 claims amounting to $139,954.
I think this clearly demonstrates that the government of the day was fully justified in introducing the act and expecting it to operate soundly and to the advantage of the small businessman. I rose particularly to mention that the chambers of commerce and the unions in the Kootenays are very interested in the development of secondary industry. This act could be of assistance to persons interested in such development. I refer to small manufacturers and those interested in the development of the tourist business and recreational facilities.
Only this morning I received a letter from the Nelson Chamber of Commerce dealing with this question. We have a large smelting
February 24, 1967	COMMONS
business in the riding, a mining industry and a forest industry but there is a place for the development of secondary industry, particularly in the smaller communities. 1 will give the minister one experience of mine in this respect. I went into this question very carefully with firms in Ontario which are interested in the manufacture of furniture, because we have large quantities of excellent quality birch in the district. The birch you see in Ontario looks like weeds compared with the birch we grow in our country.
I remember on one occasion shipping ten carloads of birch logs 32 feet in length and 2 feet in diameter at the top. I mention this to illustrate the size of the timber that grows in southeastern British Columbia. Millions of feet of birch are being destroyed at the present time as a result of building the dams on the Columbia river. The timber is simply being piled up and burned. I did everything possible to get people interested in establishing a furniture industry in the district in order to use the birch and other woods there which are very suitable for the manufacture of various types of furniture. However, I was completely unsuccessful in that respect owing to the fact that for some unknown reason the Okanagan district has been declared a designated area. That is a rather ambiguous term, Mr. Speaker, but anyway it qualifies for certain assistance in the development of new industries such as write-offs, grants and so on.
There is a great demand for the development of secondary industry in the smaller communities. These industries need financial assistance in order that they may become stabilized. When the dams and other large construction projects are completed in the constituency I have the honour to represent, this program will be more necessary than ever. There are in the area people very interested in developing accommodation for tourists, particularly in the summer months. There are others interested in the development of a small pottery industry. We have in my area excellent clay which could be used in the manufacture of pottery on a small scale, something similar to what has been done in other places in Canada. We also have in our district six hot springs; two or three are owned by people who would like to develop them further. This could be done if they were extended credit under the provisions of this act.
I mention these matters to bring them to the minister's attention and arouse his sympathy with respect to the needs of the district I
Small Businesses Loans Act Amendment have the honour to represent. I shall be writing him later on this question to see what he can propose with respect to the development of secondary industry and business in Kootenay West and Kootenay East. The people of these two constituencies are working together on these problems because they affect the whole area as a region rather than just one constituency.

Mr. Speaker, I said a few words on this subject when we were at the resolution stage. We put forward some suggestions then which I thought would be implemented with regard to areas in which the provisions of the bill might be improved to make it more acceptable and used to a greater extent than has been the case in the past. We appreciate the increase in the number of people who will be able to benefit from this legislation, but we wonder whether the loan ceiling of $25,000 is realistic. If it was realistic in 1960 I do not think it is realistic in 1967, particularly when one considers the construction, transportation and communications industries and others of that size which need a great deal more money than the ordinary retail merchant or the small manufacturer.
I was hoping that when the minister spoke today he would deal with this question. When the parliamentary secretary to the minister spoke at the resolution stage on February 16 he said, as reported at page 13141 of Hansard: All the more reason why we must expect businesses needing over $25,000 and those having a turnover exceeding $500,000 to have plans that require financing beyond the scope of the Small Businesses Loans Act.
After all, Mr. Speaker, if we are going to raise the potential turnover of a small business to $500,000, in my opinion a maximum loan of $25,000 is not sufficient. I have often wondered whether the government has considered applying a scale of charges whereby a certain interest percentage would apply on the first $25,000 and then there would be a small increase in the percentage on, say, a further $25,000. If this were done I believe more people would participate in the program and it would be more beneficial to those in the construction and transportation businesses in particular. Twenty five thousand dollars would not buy a bulldozer for use in the construction business, or a cement mixer or large machinery of this type, and in the transportation business many trucks cannot be bought for $25,000.
13460	COMMONS
Small Businesses Loans Act Amendment
I wonder whom the government discussed these amendments with and whether they went to the Retail Merchants Association, the chambers of commerce and people interested in small business to obtain their ideas as to ways and means to make the legislation more workable. The parliamentary secretary also said when speaking on this matter at the resolution stage, as reported at page 13140 of Hansard:
Of course, it is not an unimportant amount and it has probably been quite beneficial to borrowers. But it might be possible that it is not a valid sign of the entire potential demand which could exist for such loans.
He was there referring to the amount of money which had been lent under this program. So the government admits that there is a potential demand for more loans. When the hon. member for Kootenay West was speaking I was thinking of the suggestion I made in this connection. I suggested that perhaps a certain amount of the fund be set aside to provide working capital, because in small businesses this is an area where businessmen experience difficulty. To become established and obtain credit takes a certain length of time, and the small businessman often finds himself in trouble in this respect for one, two or three years. He experiences difficulty because he does not have enough working capital to carry him over this critical period. These are two important areas which have not been covered in this bill.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
There is one other matter which I should like to raise at this time. The parliamentary secretary indicated in the statement he made at the resolution stage that he was not sure whether the rate of 5.5 per cent could be retained and that this would be decided after passage of the new Bank Act. Now that the Bank Act bill is out of the committee I wonder whether the minister could give us a more definite statement on what the rate on these loans will be. Will it stay at 5.5 per cent or wiU it go up to 6.5 per cent? It has to be kept in mind that a lower rate of interest on these small business loans will make it possible for more people to participate. I hope that before second reading of the bill the minister will take note of our suggestions and give them his consideration.

speakeroldname: Mr. B. S. Mackasey (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
13462	COMMONS
Small Businesses Loans Act Amendment which will be coming before us, in the discussion of which in the finance committee I have been privileged to participate, indicate that the chartered banks of Canada have a particular role in our economy. They are synonymous in our thinking with stability. We are very proud of their record compared with that of the banks in other countries.
On the other side of the coin I think that the banking institutions of this country have a responsibility to Canadians and that responsibility extends as well to small businessmen. Some of the speeches made at the resolution stage by the hon. member for Wellington-Huron (Mr. Howe) and other Conservative members, as well as by the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Saltsman) and other members of the New Democratic Party, indicate that they have the same idea as I do that the banks have a moral obligation to help the small businessman. There are, I believe, close to 500,000 small businesses in this country which are not getting a fair share of the banking facilities that are supposed to be at their disposal. I am not sure what the solution is. I suggest to the minister that he take a good look at the interest rate. I cannot understand those in this house who believe they are helping the small businessman by setting the interest rate as low as possible. If they would talk to these businessmen on the week ends they would find that the barrier these people face is not the interest rate but how they can get their hands on money from the chartered banks or other institutions of which they are a little suspicious, perhaps unjustly so.
While I endorse the amendments I believe they in no way shape or form overcome the weaknesses which existed in the act, one of which is indicated by the reluctance of the chartered banks to co-operate or to live up to their moral obligations so that the small businessman in each community has a chance to grow. I would have liked to see some provision in the act which would have permitted small businesses to obtain funds for mergers with other small businesses. Big businesses merge and unify. One of the problems of the small businessman is that he has surplus capacity sometimes or lacks a sales staff and this could be rectified easily by merging with another small business. I think that this might have been one welcome addition to the act.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I hope the minister will realize that on the one hand we sponsor the Industrial Development Bank
[Mr. Mackasey.l
DEBATES	February 24, 1967
from which one can obtain a loan at a rate of well over 8 per cent, whereas the chartered banks can provide this service at a rate of interest that is lower. However, the small businessman cannot get a loan there. If this act is going to be of service to the small businessman, then we have to be very realistic about setting a rate of interest, a prerogative which lies with the minister. Secondly, we have to use some type of moral suasion on the chartered banks to co-operate for the benefit of the small businessman.

Mr. Speaker, I want to speak very briefly in support of the principle of the bill now before the house. Like the family farm to which we have made reference on so many occasions, small business has been in the past and continues to be one of the important and desirable factors in our economic life. We all know that in recent years there has been an increasing emphasis on business. This is true in practically every phase of life. We talk about big business, big firms and big products. This type of thinking has even moved into ecclesiastical circles. We talk about big church organizations. My theory is that there is a danger in equating the idea of size with efficiency and progress. I suggest it is not always indicative of efficiency or progress. People put huge units in opposition to small units in our society.
In my view the so-called small businessman has made and continues to make a very worth-while contribution to our way of life. He should be encouraged and assisted in the efforts he is putting forth. When my colleague the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke (Mr. Johnston) spoke at the resolution stage of the bill he referred to the fact that on many occasions the small businessman operates as a convenience to the respective communities in which he may function. Unfortunately, I suggest that too many of us just use the small businessman as a convenience after the large business places have closed for the night or when the housewife runs short of one or two items. In such case the comer grocer is very convenient. However, we think he should be more than a convenience and as such he should receive encouragement and assistance in carrying on his operations. Not only does he provide a convenience but he also provides a personalized service in many cases which is not found in the larger units. I am sure we all appreciate the fact that these
February 24, 1967	COMMONS
businessmen who operate in our communities are providing a service that is not only convenient but is personalized as well.
I believe, as I have said, that we must do everything we possibly can to assist the small businessman to carry on his operations, make a living for himself and his family and make the contribution to the community he desires to make. The small businessman is not there just to make money. It is true that he has to make money in order to survive and provide for himself, but I believe he takes pride in being part of the community and rendering a service. I believe we all appreciate and recognize that. Perhaps we should recognize the additional burdens that are placed not only upon him but on larger units as well. The small businessman has had to become a bookkeeper for the government with regard to pensions, taxes and all these other things. He is burdened to a considerable extent with bookkeeping, accounting and other activities on behalf not of himself but of various levels of government. Perhaps there should be some way in which this is recognized when he is taking care of his tax return.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
I believe there are other ways in which he should be assisted, but I think that the provision of capital is a very essential requirement. A short time ago I read that there are approximately 4,000 small businesses which go out of business every year, and I think this is a rather serious situation. I realize many reasons may contribute to business failure. For example, perhaps a businessman did not make sufficient preparation before going into business to assure that he would be able to continue his operations. Perhaps he did not have enough capital in the first place in order to provide adequate facilities.
Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that inability to acquire sufficient capital at various stages of a business operation is one of the factors which forces the small businessman to the wall and which puts him on the labour market. He must have access to sources of capital to meet emergencies which may arise. He must have sufficient capital to expand his business or to face the competition that he meets today. Some small business operators say that they are not afraid of competition from large concerns if only they are able to obtain the capital required to expand their business facilities to meet that competition. I think it is absolutely essential that they do receive the assistance that is required in this connection. Then, of course, working
Small Businesses Loans Act Amendment capital is also necessary to help small businesses to continue to serve their community and help our economy.
As I have said, Mr. Speaker, we support the principle of the measure now before us. However, even though there has been some expansion of the categories of businesses covered by the legislation, I think the legislation is still too restrictive. There are other types of business operations that I believe should be incorporated within the provisions of this bill. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, although the minister has widened the legislation a little further this time I hope that in the very near future he will see fit to bring others within its scope. As I have said, it is still too difficult to obtain capital not only under this legislation but also under other pieces of legislation.
Reference has been made today to the Industrial Development Bank. Relatively small businessmen or industrialists have approached the bank for loans, yet there seems to be a repetition of the old saying that if you do not need money you can get it, but that if you do need money you cannot get it. This has apparently been the experience of all too many in their endeavours to secure capital under the provisions of various pieces of legislation, and I believe it is also true in this particular case.
The hon. member who preceded me pointed out that perhaps part of the responsibility lies with the banks, because of their hesitancy in lending money under the interest rate prescribed. Perhaps they are more interested in lending large sums than small sums, owing to the cost of administration. Nevertheless I believe it is still too difficult for small businessmen to obtain the capital that is required, and that we ought to accommodate them in this regard by enabling them to borrow the money required to carry on their operations.
We have noted the increase in the estimated gross revenue from $250,000 to $500,000. Perhaps smaller businesses are more in need than those with a gross revenue above $250,000. However, Mr. Speaker, as I say, we support this particular provision. On the other hand we also put in an extra plug for the more humble businessmen, because of their greater need. We support of course the extension of the operations of this act for a further period, and we may have some other comments to make when the bill is before committee of the whole.

Mr. Speaker, my remarks will be brief.
13464	COMMONS
Small Businesses Loans Act Amendment Naturally I support the proposals made by the minister as far as they go, but I submit that they do not go quite far enough. I assume the minister will agree that perhaps the act has not been made use of to the extent that was anticipated when it was passed. The mere fact that the original limit on loans set in the act was $300 million over a period of three years and that up to the end of 1965 only $127 million of that amount had been taken up is an indication of this. This means that an amount of $25 million a year or so is being taken up.
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, the number of loans which are being made seems extremely small, something in the order of 2,000 to 3,000 per year. Obviously there must be some reason why this act has not been used to the extent anticipated. I realize that the purposes for which loans can be made are limited and no doubt this has been a factor. Therefore a broadening of the act in this respect by the present bill is commendable.
Like the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Macaluso) I also have the feeling that in many cases banks have been rather loath to lend money under this act. In some instances I know that banks have talked the proposed borrower out of obtaining a loan under the terms of this act and have given him a loan under the provisions of the Bank Act. I am not a suggesting that the minister should raise the rate, but I think he could inquire whether banks are prepared to lend money at the rate prescribed. It would be more advantageous for a small businessman to get a loan even at a slightly higher rate than to be unable to get a loan at all.
My main criticism of this bill, Mr. Speaker, is that it does not increase the maximum amount of the loan that may be made. It is true that the average amount of loan up to the end of 1965 was less than $10,000. Nevertheless I have personal knowledge of at least two cases in my riding where a loan could not be obtained because an amount of more than $25,000 was required.
I have checked with officials of the minister's department, Mr. Speaker, but they have no first-hand knowledge of how many applications may have been submitted and rejected because the amount of loan was restricted to $25,000. They have no way of knowing except from inquiring of the banks how many turned down loans for this reason. Banks report to the government of course only on loans actually made.

DEBATES	February 24, 1967
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me logical that since the gross revenue has now been increased to half a million dollars from a quarter of a million, the maximum amount of loan available should be substantially increased also, and I hope the minister will give this his consideration. I see no objection to increasing the amount from $25,000 to, say, $50,000, a higher rate of interest being applied on the second half of that amount. This is being done today under the Farm Credit Act and the Veterans' Land Act. I think the minister would be well advised to increase the amount of the loan and then at his discretion to set a higher rate of interest on that part of the loan wich would exceed $25,000.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
I hope the minister will give consideration to these points and that later, in his closing speech, he will tell us, from the information he has available to him, why this act has not been used to the extent originally anticipated.

My remarks, too, will be brief. I am confident the minister will find that these proposed amendments will meet with general approval all over the country. I think it is recognized that we are a country of small businesses. I have no recent data available, but statistics published not long ago indicated that of the 37,500 manufacturing industries or establishments in existence at that time some 35,000 could be placed in the category of small business, employing fewer than 99 people each.
I know that in the Atlantic area from which I come, the greater the number of small and prosperous industries we have the sounder will be our economy. I often think it is better to have 20 businesses employing 50 people each than to have one employing 1,000 people. This is why I am confident that every encouragement should be given to people who wish to open small businesses and small enterprises.
There is one deficiency that I see in the act as it now exists, and I should like to draw it to the attention of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) so that he may give it whatever consideration he sees fit. As I read the act today, no provision is made for the advancement of the guarantee on loans to buy existing businesses. The amendment before us would, if it is true, allow a guaranteed loan to be made for the purpose of buying premises. If a young man wished to enter business, this loan would be available to him. Under the existing provisions he would be able to get a
February 24, 1967	COMMONS
loan in order to buy the fixtures and equipment and to make the necessary renovations. But as the act is drafted at present I see nothing which would allow the banks to guarantee a loan for the purchase of an existing business. I think this is an important consideration because there are many young men who would like to enter the small business field, and who see an opportunity to do so when someone who has been engaged in a particular enterprise wishes to get out of it.
Unfortunately, even with the amendment proposed today by the minister, a guaranteed loan cannot be made for this purpose under the act. I would therefore suggest to the minister that it would be of tremendous benefit to small enterprise if now, while we have the act open, some provision could be made whereby a guaranteed loan could be obtained from the banks for the purpose I have outlined.

wish to make a few comments of a general nature on this bill. I presume we shall shortly begin a clause by clause discussion.
The purpose of the bill before us is limited. It extends the provisions of the Small Businesses Loans Act to construction, transportation or communications. It extends the duration of the act and expands its scope so as to include the purchase and construction of premises. There are two matters I should like to refer to the minister's attention and the first relates to the limitations which are placed on the amount of the loan which can be made.
When the original bill was passed some five years ago, $25,000 was considered adequate for what the government had in mind. At that time there was no other fund to which small business could turn for public assistance. This applied particularly to the type of business in which I am interested, the resort business and the service industry. The bill did serve a purpose, though perhaps it has not been as successful as we had hoped.
I think the time has come when we should expand the provisions of this act far beyond anything the present bill proposes. I believe we should raise the ceiling on these loans because $25,000 is not enough in the case of many of these businesses. I believe the time has come when provision should be made for refinancing. In my view the only reason the small Businesses Loans Act has not been as successful as originally hoped is that in many cases the people who make application for loans need to pay off smaller existing encumbrances before proceeding with the work they
Small Businesses Loans Act Amendment have in mind. I may say there are very few businesses today which do not have some sort of mortgage or encumbrance against them.
As the bill now reads, the full amount made available must be used for the purpose of the construction and modernizing of premises; none of it can be used for refinancing. There certainly has to be a limit but I think, for a reason. I shall mention in a few moments, that the time has come to permit a certain amount of refinancing to be undertaken.
I say this because the only other source of guaranteed government loans available to most people, the Industrial Development Bank seems now to be restricting its credit to small businessmen. Both the Small Businesses Loans Act and the Industrial Development Bank have their shortcomings. The former does not permit the use of any money for refinancing. The I.D.B. does, but it has been my experience in the last year or so that the bank has been greatly restricting its loans to private industry and to small business. Indeed, loans have been restricted to the point at which the system has lost its effectiveness. There is a wide gap at the present time between transactions which are covered by the Small Businesses Loans Act and those which are handled by the I.D.B. Years ago there were signs that the Industrial Development Bank would be useful to small manufacturing firms, small tourist industries and the like. But during the past year there has been a change of attitude or a change of direction. Time after time I have been unsuccessful in getting the bank to do what the act it should do-assist in development.
The people running it have established themselves as bankers and they are not doing the development job they should be doing for small business. I do not wish to go too deeply into this aspect of the subject because you might call me to order, Mr. Speaker, but I would point out again that there is a tremendous gap between what is intended under the Small Businesses Loans Act and what the I.D.B. does. There does not need to be such a gap because there is sufficient authority under this Act to permit loans for the expansion of premises, and there is authority vested in the Industrial Development Bank to handle a lot of industrial loans. The authority is there but it is not being used.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
I can think of four or five industries which are ready to move, but which have been tied up with Industrial Development Bank red
13466	COMMONS
Small Businesses Loans Act Amendment tape, to the point where they cannot do their job. The bank is acting as a banker and not as an agency of the government. For this reason I appeal to the minister to close the existing gap between the Small Businesses Loans Act and the I.D.B. The authority exists. The idea is to help the businesses that want to begin or improve production in Canada, also to help our export business.
Let me give an example of the gap existing between the provisions of this bill and the functions of the I.D.B. A company manufacturing entirely for export applied to the I.D.B. for a loan. At that time it had received a letter from the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters) asking it to step up its export business for the 1967 centennial year. The company had also applied to the area development agency, and had been approved. The Minister of Trade and Commerce had requested it to set up its business, the area development agency had authorized it to proceed with expansion, but the I.D.B. procrastinated for six months, fooling around with red tape. Eventually the firm had to abandon the expansion for 1967. All its business was export business.
A gap exists, and needs to be closed. I could cite other examples, and I have already spoken to the minister about one or two instances. I feel, and feel strongly, that the Industrial Development Bank is not doing its job, and that the Small Businesses Loans Act is not functioning in those areas where the bank does not function. Between the I.D.B. and Small Businesses Loans Act, and their failure to meet certain needs, the development of industry, in Canada, particularly small industry, is being held back. I do not know what can be done to persuade them.
I appeal to the minister to do what he can to make the Small Businesses Loans Act as effective as possible. If the measure before us is all that can be proposed at this time, then let us pass it. If the Industrial Development Bank will not do the job it was set up to do namely, development loans, then the Small Businesses Loans Act should be expanded to do the job the bank ought to do. The bank tangles everybody in red tape.
Let me cite another example. The company in question tried for six months to obtain a loan. In February of 1966 the company applied to the I.D.B. for a development loan. The bank did nothing until November. When the Ontario development agency was set up the company went to it and obtained a loan in three weeks. The point is that the I.D.B.

DEBATES	February 24, 1967
ought to have provided that loan. This is just one example out of half a dozen.
I know that the minister does not tell the I.D.B. how to run its show. He does not like to tell the bank to make a loan to this or that person. If he did that sort of thing it would put all its applications on his desk. Nevertheless I appeal to the minister to tell the bank to get off its rear end and to help develop industry in this country.

speechtext: If the minister speaks now he will close the debate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank hon. members who have contributed to this debate. My reply will be brief. A good deal has been said about the size of loans and whether it would not be wise in this act to increase the limit above $25,000, just as we have increased the eligibility of businesses by increasing the volume of business that makes them eligible from $250,000 to $500,000.
It will interest the house to know that in the last three years the average size of a loan under this act has been less than $10,000, though the upper limit was $25,000. It is even more interesting to note that the great bulk of loans has been in the range $5,000 to $15,000, which shows that the upper limit of the size of loans has not been a particularly limiting factor. Indeed the demand has been for much smaller loans.
Somebody asked whether the proposed amendments had been discussed with the retail merchants. I can answer in the affirmative. The Retail Merchants Association of Canada made representations to the government that the upper limit should be $50,000 rather than $25,000. The association on examination, however, was unable really to substantiate the need for the increase in the upper limit. Indeed they said that they would consider an increase of much smaller proportions to be quite adequate.
We did consider the possibility of raising the limit above $25,000, but in the light of the figures I have given to the house I think it will be understood that we do not consider that this was a major factor affecting the usefulness of this legislation.
Various members have spoken about the rate of interest. There has been general support for greater flexibility in the interest rate, that the banks might be encouraged to make loans to businesses under the guarantee provided by the act. Until the Bank Act provisions
February 24, 1967	COMMONS
are approved it will be difficult to know on what basis to fix the rate of interest.
May I suggest to the house three general considerations that I believe are highly relevant and that will to a large extent govern the regulations when they are ultimately promulgated. I think the maximum rate should be sufficiently high to preclude the banks discriminating against the use of this guaranteed facility by small business, in favour of other borrowers. Second, the rate must be lower than the rate at which banks normally lend to businesses by a differential wide enough to preclude the banks putting all small business loans under the guarantee.
The original .5 per cent differential below the prevailing rate achieved this end. Of course, if the banks are given greater freedom under the Bank Act the rates will have to be changed accordingly. We believe too that there should not be too wide a difference between the rate under this legislation and the Industrial Development Bank rate on small loans.
As hon. members know, the I.D.B. rate at present is around 7.5 per cent to 8 per cent. Loans have recently been made at higher rates. I can assure the house that the interest rate will be looked at in the light of making the act as widely available to small businesses as possible.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
The hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Aiken) voiced complaints about the activities of the Industrial Development Bank. Since you did not choose to consider this as being out of order, Mr. Speaker, perhaps I might be permitted to make a brief reply. As the hon. member said, the Minister of Finance does not govern the activities of the Industrial Development Bank, and I do not believe he should. I believe there is a good deal of advantage in having the Industrial Development Bank removed from political pressures, by having it a subsidiary of the Bank of Canada. However, it will interest my hon. friend to know that representations were made to me the other day by an association of financial companies complaining to me that the Industrial Development Bank was being so active in the financing of small businesses that in fact it was taking business away from organizations which would be able to do the job, if only they were not subjected to such unfair competition from a government agency. So, Mr. Speaker, I think there are two sides to this problem.
Small Businesses Loans Act Amendment

Mr. Speaker, may I ask the minister a question, more or less in clarification. Would he not agree that if the Industrial Development Bank would limit itself to those companies who need some assistance in their development, then the ordinary lending institutions could handle loans which are easily within the limitations of commercial transactions. In other words the Industrial Development Bank and the Small Businesses Loans Act administration could assist many of the companies which otherwise could not get credit. In fact the Industrial Development Bank is involved in these safe loans and is leaving alone the marginal businesses which should be helped.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will see that the comments of the hon. gentleman are brought to the attention of the bank. Generally the question has been asked, why is the act not being used as extensively as it might be. There are several reasons. First of all I believe that the range of businesses which are eligible for loans has not been as wide as it should be. The purpose of this bill is to correct that defect. Second, I believe monetary conditions have developed in such a way that the banks have not had the incentives which they might have had to make loans under the provisions of this legislation.
When the Bank Act revisions are made I hope the regulations in respect of the interest rate will be such that they will provide the banks with the necessary incentive to ensure that small businesses do obtain the advantage of the government guarantee which is available under this legislation.
Finally, questions were asked concerning the reason the provisions of this act are not available for the establishment of new businesses. I can only reply that that is not its purpose. It was not introduced for that purpose. I believe it would be a mistake to enlarge this act so that it would enable people who are not now in business to finance the establishment of a business. There are other facilities which exist for that purpose, notably the Industrial Development Bank. If we feel, however, that existing facilities are not adequate for the purpose, I suggest that we should look to legislation other than the Small Businesses Loans Act for the remedy.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Batten in the Chair.

Small Businesses Loans Act Amendment

In my remarks I said that I wondered whether in respect of these amendments the minister would consider the possibility of increasing the amount of the loan. This has been suggested by the Retail Merchants Association. I wonder whether consideration might be given to raising the amount of the loan and charging a little extra interest for the extra $10,000, $15,000 or $25,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, as members of the committee probably realize, this is only one means by which small businesses can be financed. The purpose is to provide loans of up to $25,000 at preferred rates of interest because of the existence of the government guarantee. I do not think any purpose would be served by having a higher rate of interest on loans in larger amounts. That in fact now is provided for by the banks themselves, which can lend any amount of money they wish to a business, and charge what rate of interest they will within the law. I suggest to the hon. member that his suggestion would not be a practical way to accomplish his purpose. Had we thought that the $25,000 limitation was unnecessary under present circumstances, or undesirable, we would have altered it. Our analysis, however, showed that it was not the size of the loan which limited the usefulness of the act.
Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether the minister would like to clarify his statement to the effect that the banks could charge what they will.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I said, "within the law". The banks, however, can make loans to these businesses without the government guarantee provided by the act. The banks are free to charge what they will within the law.

Mr. Chairman, I have one short question which I should like to address to the minister. Would the minister inform the house whether banks or other lending institutions can refuse a loan, even though the borrower qualifies for it but is not a customer of that bank or lending institution? Would such a reason enable a bank or other lending institution to refuse the loan.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is nothing in this act which compels a bank to make a loan. So I think I must say that the answer to that question is yes. The purpose of this act is to provide guarantees to banks so that they will

DEBATES	February 24, 1967
be more disposed to make loans. I do not think we could pass legislation which would require a bank to make a loan.

Mr. Chairman, the minister has broadened this act to include construction, transportation and communication. I am wondering whether he would give consideration to extending the guaranteed loan provisions of this act to cover loans made to medical and dental clinics. I am sure that if the minister would pause to reflect on the situation which exists across our country, he would realize there is a great lack in the field of medical and dental facilities. All of us are aware that there are many young graduates who wish to start a practice in the medical or dental profession who find that the cost of setting up such practice, with the cost of new equipment today being what it is, is terrific.
In the dental field I believe the desired requirement for dentists is that there be one for every 1,000 persons. We are a long way from reaching that target. I believe there is only one dentist for about every 3,000 persons. If we look at the figures in respect of the medical profession, I think we would find that the percentage would be about the same.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)

REVISION OF LAW ON EAVESDROPPING THROUGH WIRE TAPPING
speechtext:
second reading of Bill No. C-33, to amend the Criminal Code (wire tapping, etc.).
He said: The purpose of this bill, Mr. Speaker, is to amend the Criminal Code in order to revise the old common law offence of *eavesdropping. At the present time the only penalty for wire tapping is to be found in the various provincial telephone acts wherein the penalty ranges from a maximum of six months imprisonment in Manitoba to a maximum of one month in Ontario. Some of the other provincial telephone acts contain no provision for dealing with this type of offence.
The greatest testimony to the value of this bill is the fact that the bill was originally introduced into this house by the present Solicitor General (Mr. Pennell) before he took that important office. When he became Solicitor General, I looked at the bill and made certain small revisions in it. It is now evident that in many parts of Canada eavesdropping, wire tapping or electronic bugging as it has been called, is being carried on very extensively both by police agencies and private organizations.
Some weeks ago the Attorney General of the Province of Ontario, Mr. Wishart, admitted in the Ontario legislature that the Ontario Provincial Police were involved in wire tapping. He made the comment that he urged the federal government to amend the Criminal Code to permit wire tapping by police and law enforcement agencies under certain conditions. He urged the federal government to outline the conditions under which such wire tapping would be permissible. While I am not certain, Mr. Speaker, that it is really necessary for the police to have this authority, I do recognize the problem which police and law enforcement agencies have to face. I have therefore included in clause 2 of this bill a provision which would spell out the right of the police to appear before a judge of a superior court, to give the judge reasons for requiring the right to wire tap, and for the

judge to grant an order giving the police such right.
The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that in the last couple of years, from one end of Canada to the other, we have had evidence that wire tapping is being used. It is being used in a way which infringes very definitely, I submit, the fundamental right which every citizen ought to have to privacy. In British Columbia there is now a royal commission investigating wire tapping. I do not want to comment on the reasons which led to the establishment of the royal commission, nor do I want to say anything about what the royal commission may find. I do want to say that an R.C.M.P. officer made a statement before the royal commission that he had received training in the R.C.M.P. organization on methods of wire tapping. He had been involved in wiretapping, not in the particular case being investigated but in other cases.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
In the city of Saskatoon evidence came to light several years ago that the only telephone which could be used by people who were locked up in the city jail had been so "looked after" that the police could listen in and record conversations by prisoners, or people kept in custody even though not convicted, including conversations of a confidential nature with lawyers. I submit that this is quite improper.
During the hearings before Mr. Justice Dorion in the province of Quebec the R.C.M.P. officers gave evidence that they had equipment which they can and do use to record conversations carried on over the telephone. During the time of the F.L.Q. bombings-and I do not for a moment minimize the seriousness of those occurrences and the difficulties experienced by the police-according to the information I have, police officials in the city of Montreal tapped at least 200 telephones in order to attempt to get information about the people involved.
It may be that these techniques are necessary, Mr. Speaker. If they are, I submit that it is incumbent upon the police and the attorney general of a province, as well as upon the Minister of Justice (Mr. Cardin) and the Solicitor General (Mr. Pennell), to make a case that they are necessary. First of all, they should change the law to permit wire tapping. Second, there should be included in such changes methods by which the police and other agencies with legitimate cause to wire tap can do so legally. I submit that unless this
February 24, 1967	COMMONS
is done it is not only morally wrong but is indefensible and should be prohibited by law.
In 1964 a Toronto Star columnist, Mr. Ron Haggart, disclosed detailed information about wire tapping by R.C.M.P. officers in the city to Toronto. The leader of this party, the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas), as well as myself, asked detailed questions of the then minister of justice, and this practice was denied. Yet both Mr. Haggart and a responsible lawyer in Toronto, Mr. Frank Nasso, wrote to me giving the details. I submitted the letter of Mr. Nasso and the columns written by Mr. Haggart to the then minister of justice. I know he had his difficulties and became ill later, but he never did reply to the very serious charges being made that wire tapping was going on.
Not only that, Mr. Speaker, but the minister of justice at that time denied that the man named in the charges was an official of the R.C.M.P. According to Mr. Nasso, this man stated that the owners of the building had given him permission to instal wire tapping equipment because he was investigating an excise case. In fact he never did have the permission of the building owners and in fact was trespassing, yet nothing was done. The matter was ignored by the minister of justice, who as I say never did reply to my letters.
I might also mention, Mr. Speaker, that the Bell Telephone Company admitted that even if they had received information that the police were engaged in wire tapping they would not have instituted any action that would lead to prosecution of the police. Perhaps this is understandable from the point of view of the Bell Telephone Company or any other company, because there are no laws to prohibit wire tapping. This is the purpose of my bill, Mr. Speaker.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that there is sufficient evidence today that wire tapping is carried on both by the police and by private agencies. There is no law to prohibit it. If wire tapping is a necessary practice, then the Criminal Code should be amended to spell out to the people of Canada that this practice is necessary. It should not only detail when wire tapping is necessary but why it is necessary, and it should outline the kind of steps police or any other agencies which require to engage upon wire tapping should and must take before they carry on their operations.
I submit that the implications of wire tapping are so serious that it ought not to be permitted without an order from a supreme court judge, and this is precisely what I am suggesting.
Criminal Code Amendment
As I said earlier, Mr. Speaker, the principle contained in this bill was introduced into the house and endorsed by the present Solicitor General. It has also been endorsed and adopted by newspaper editors from one end of Canada to the other.
Before I sit down, Mr. Speaker, I want to put on the record very briefly the views of some newspaper editorial writers in this country, both Liberal and Conservative in allegiance. The Toronto Globe and Mail for December 9, 1966 carried an editorial headed "Laws for dangerous snoops", and I should like to read the last paragraph:
Obviously, there is a need for laws to restrain electronic eavesdropping-not just for private individuals, but for the police, the military, and everyone. Bugging is an invasion of individual privacy; the dangers of permitting such an invasion to go unchecked are far greater than those involved in depriving private and public investigative agencies of a useful tool.
An editorial entitled "The big ear is listening" appeared in the Toronto Star on September 5, 1964 and carried the following statement:
What is needed is an amendment to the Criminal Code that would ban all electronic or mechanical eavesdropping. The only exception would be made for police eavesdropping with the permission of a superior court judge.
This is precisely what I am proposing, Mr. Speaker.
In an editorial headed "Wire tapping" in the Toronto Telegram for Friday, May 13, 1966, which was after the Solicitor General had been asked questions about wire tapping, questions which he did not answer, three choices are listed for the minister which I think are quite logical and commend to him, though unfortunately he is not here this afternoon. They are as follows:
1.	If the R.C.M.P. resorts to wire tapping, which is illegal under the Criminal Code,-
I interject to say that I think they are wrong in this regard, too.
he must put an end to this practice, for the force is breaking the law. He should also announce this action to parliament and the country.
2.	If the R.C.M.P. is not engaged in wire tapping, he should clear it of this suspicion at once by making a statement in parliament.
3.	If Mr. Pennell believes that wire tapping is a necessary method of investigation, he should admit this. He should then introduce legislation to make it legal for the R.C.M.P. and other police forces to carry on this practice.
It has been suggested, Mr. Speaker, that we cannot deal with this question because the royal commission on security will be dealing
February 24, 19S7

Criminal Code Amendment with it. That may well be so. However, I submit that if the law enforcement agencies of this country believe that in security cases the police require to resort to wire tapping, then they ought to say so. This contention is not in contradistinction to what I am proposing in this bill. If the law enforcement agencies can prove a case, then I submit that by passing this bill parliament can give them the right to take action.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
I submit in closing that it is wrong for police agents no matter how responsible they may be to arrogate to themselves the right to decide when and where and in what circumstances they will listen to telephone conversations carried on by any citizen of this country, because I submit there is not a person in this chamber or outside this house who cannot remember at least one occasion on which he discussed matters over the telephone which would be extremely embarrassing if they came to the attention of any other person. I submit that this kind of eavesdropping is wrong in principle and that it should be stopped, and this is the purpose of my appeal.

subtopic: REVISION OF LAW ON EAVESDROPPING THROUGH WIRE TAPPING
speechtext:
I want to take a few minutes in which to consider what is involved in the bill before us. The hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) has used many arguments in favour of the principle of the bill but I think there is probably no one in this chamber who would disagree with that principle. There are, however, some details on which I have suggestions to make.
My primary criticism, indeed, is that the bill does not go far enough. I would prefer that this house were dealing with Bill C-45, the bill introduced by the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. Stanbury) which covers such things as electronic listening devices which are not dealt with here. However, the principle is good and it is really not necessary to convince those of us who sit on this side of the house that in principle this is desirable legislation and a good step to take.
Nevertheless, I would suggest to the hon. member, though I realize he will not agree with me, that it would be prudent and wise for us on this side of the house, and indeed for all hon. members, to wait until the commission which will undoubtedly consider these questions in relation to national security has reported. We might also do well to wait until the royal commission set up by the British Columbia government has completed

its work. It is fair to say that the hon. member has ancitipated this suggestion because he himself referred to the commission set up in British Columbia.
I might also say that I am generally in favour of this bill because there is some confusion attaching to the legal aspects of intrusions on privacy. There are areas with which our common law does not deal and with regard to which we have no legislation. The bill before us will make it an offence, not being a sender or receiver of a telephone or telegraph communication to wilfully, and by means of an instrument-this is where I criticize the measure as being too narrow in its application-intercept, or record a telephone or telegraph communication. Then the penalties are set out and provision is made for an exception by authority of an order of a judge of a superior court. A further provision makes it an offence, except in certain circumstances, to disclose any information concerning the application for the granting or denial of an order.
I wish to refer quickly to the law in the United Kingdom because I think it is in a more satisfactory state in this area than is our law in Canada.

subtopic: REVISION OF LAW ON EAVESDROPPING THROUGH WIRE TAPPING
speechtext: We can learn a lot from the United Kingdom.

subtopic: REVISION OF LAW ON EAVESDROPPING THROUGH WIRE TAPPING
speechtext:
I have to agree with the hon. member. This is one of the reasons I am taking a minute or two to review their law. There are very few of us in this house, certainly very few common law lawyers in this house, who would argue with the hon. member when he says we can learn a good deal from the mother country in regard to the law.
The origin of the power to intercept communications can only be surmised, but this power has been recognized from very early times and has been recognized as lawful by a succession of statutes covering the last 200 years or more. There is some difference of view among United Kingdom lawyers as to the authority to intercept telephone messages.
According to one view, this power is identical with the power to open letters and rests on the ancient power to intercept communications. Another view is that it derives from statutory authority. The power to intercept communications is exercised in the United Kingdom for the prevention and detection of serious crime and for the preservation of the safety of the state.
Turning from this brief summary of the United Kingdom law, I note that the sponsor
February 24, 1967	COMMONS
of this bill has already alluded to the unsatisfactory situation in Canada where we have left what little legislation there is to be enacted by the provincial legislatures. The law in Canada is not nearly as clear as it appears to be in the United Kingdom. As I have said, the English law seems to base the power of the executive to intercept communications upon the power to open letters. The only statute we appear to have in Canada under federal authority, and which might be relevant, is section 41 of the Post Office Act, chapter 212 of the Statutes of Canada, 1952. There is no power under that act at all to intercept or open letters, except letters coming into Canada, even by police or government agencies for the purpose of national security.
Thus, we do not have this parallel power upon which the law in the United Kingdom is founded. The prohibition against interception of telegraphic and telephonic communication seems to be broader and I can refer the house to section 6 of the Telegraphs Act, chapter 262 of the Statutes of Canada, 1952. There is a good case for some form of legislation in Canada if for no other reason than to clarify the law.
It is undoubtedly the case that certain segments of the criminal element exploit the practice of wire tapping for illegal purposes. The problem is likely to be a growing one, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North said. It is likely to increase to an alarming degree. Provisions should be set out in the law to deal with electronic devices. The use of anything being used for the interception of telephonic or telegraphic communications should be rigidly controlled by an act of this parliament. To justify interference with the privacy and liberty of the individual Canadian there must be strict proof for the necessity of such interference. This proof must be established before a competent judicial authority.
I shall have something to say about this point in just a moment. I think we ought to follow the broad principle covered by my remarks. The power of interception should be granted and used for the prevention and detection of serious crime and for the preservation of the safety of the nation.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
I shall go into detail. My criticisms, I hope will be taken as constructive criticisms, because I do not criticize the principle of the bill. Clause 2 seeks to add section 429A to the Criminal Code. It seems to me that it would not be advisable to require proof only of
Criminal Code Amendment offences punishable by ten years imprisonment. Offences with a lesser punishment ought to be included under these provisions. For instance, we might consider frauds upon the government, municipal corruption as defined under sections 102 and 104 of the Criminal Code; we might consider the sending of false messages, or indecent and threatening telephone calls dealt with under sections 315 and 316 of the Criminal Code. We might also deal with organized gambling, under the gambling provisions of the code. All these offences carry penalties of less than ten years. I think the Criminal Code should be amended in the way I have suggested, to bring in these lesser offences. On some of these lesser offences it might be proper to make application for an order giving power to eavesdrop.
Another criticism I have is that in clause 2 the application must be made before a judge of superior court jurisdiction. This ought to be considered further. I do not say this order should be returnable before a justice of the peace, as under section 429, of the Criminal Code. Search warrants are obtained from a justice of the peace. I think the order should be made returnable to an official higher than a justice of the peace, but lower than a superior court judge. In some areas of Canada it is often difficult to have access to a judge of the superior court. It seems to me that we could rely on the judicial function of a county or district court judge. County judges should have concurrent jurisdiction with superior court judges. This is important, as I said, because it is often difficult to have access to judges of superior court jurisdiction.
The other matter I mention criticizes a detail of the bill, not its principle. Again I refer to clause 2. It seems to me the provision that the order extend for one month is much too rigid. I suggest to the sponsor that this provision would inhibit the investigation of suspected offences. I think a three month order ought to be considered; possibly a six month order would be better. The investigating officials would not be hampered by having to come back to a judge after a month for an extension of the original order.
I conclude by saying that in principle I think this legislation is desirable. I think the bill ought to go farther than it does. It should cover items of electronic intrusion I mentioned earlier. All hon. members should support the measure when the point is reached where the house may make a decision. That point will probably be reached when we are
February 24, 1967

Criminal Code Amendment able to read the report of the royal commission dealing with security matters, and after we have given the commission an opportunity to recommend what should be done about the matters we are now considering. We should also read the report of the British Columbia royal commission on this subject. As I say, when we have read these reports we shall be in a position to enact legislation along the lines of the bill before us.
For the reasons I have already suggested, the bill should be changed. In general, however, the legislation should be enacted. It should be operative in respect of the new devices of this electronic age which intrude on the privacy of the Canadian people.

It was, he said, the right to khold a conversation without being spied on.
Commissioner R. A. Sargent said he wasn't trying to start an argument, but in his view it would be difficult to legally define the meaning of the word "privacy". "It can take many forms," he said.
Replied Webster: "To me any person who eavesdrops without authority, by electronic device, is guilty of invasion of privacy."
The fact was later brought out that unfortunately a corporal of the R.C.M.P. and a former member of the force co-operated together to advise Mr. Pat O'Neal, as he was then known, how to proceed to bug a convention being held by another union. That is, of course, the reason for the investigation being conducted in Vancouver. We cannot say very much about that investigation, we have to await the report of the commissioner; but it has stirred a very healthy interest in this question.
It also stirred the interest of the hon. member for Kootenay West, Mr. Speaker. I have spent over two months consulting trade unions in British Columbia, other persons and legal gentlemen who are not members of the House of Commons. On Monday I hope to introduce a bill that is the result of a considerable study of the practice in the United States and in Great Britain in dealing with this kind of issue. As I say, I hope to introduce this bill next Monday, and it will be termed an act respecting the right of privacy. I must say that this bill was not drafted off the cuff, as it were; a great deal of time was taken on this question and I consulted persons whose opinions I respect very much indeed.
Mr. Speaker, I see that the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) has now entered the chamber. I am quite confident he has something interesting to tell the house. Therefore, I again express my support for the principle of the bill and am grateful for this opportunity for members to express their opinions on it. I trust that not later than the receipt of the report of the royal commission investigating security the government will take action to amend the Criminal Code to protect the rights of all citizens of Canada.

subtopic: TABLING OF REPORT OF CARTER COMMISSION ON TAXATION

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: TABLING OF REPORT OF CARTER COMMISSION ON TAXATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with the leave of the house I should like to table the report of the Royal Commission on Taxation. It was delivered to the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) on Wednesday of this week. There are, as hon. members will see, six volumes in English. There are four full volumes here of the French version, plus the conclusions and recommendations in French of the two other volumes, namely volumes 4 and 6. When we have received volumes 4 and 6 in the French language, they will of course be tabled promptly.
As the house can plainly see, this is a very long report on the result of an inquiry that has been under way since the commissioners were appointed in September, 1962. The majority of the commission, I am informed, has recommended many novel and important changes in our tax laws, which are complicated and interrelated. It will take a long time for hon. members and the public to read these
Report of Carter Commission reports and to assess the recommendations and arguments pro and con. There will inevitably be many differing views as to what should be done about the proposals.
[DOT] (6:00 p.m.)
The government intends to study the report and the views expressed on it during the next few months, before reaching conclusions about the recommendations made by the commission or alternative suggestions from other sources. In the meantime, we do not intend to comment upon the substance of the report, nor indicate our intentions concerning its recommendations. Any premature comments, or forecasts of our intentions on these matters, could have substantial effects upon markets and upon business decisions. There will no doubt be uncertainty in some of our markets and in some industries during the period that is necessary to come to wise decisions after public discussion of these important but contentious issues.
